What makes an AI answer worth relying on?

A convincing answer and a sound reason to trust it are different things. Asking for an explanation can produce more words without settling that difference.

In March 2025, Anthropic reported tracing parts of Claude 3.5 Haiku’s internal calculations. Its method captured only a fraction of the total computation, even on short prompts.

That is partial understanding. It doesn’t tell us that a particular answer is wrong. It also doesn’t make the model’s explanation a complete account of how it reached that answer.

There’s a separate problem: whether an explanation helps someone judge the answer.

In a 199-participant study by Buçinca and colleagues, interventions prompting deliberate thought reduced overreliance more than the simple explanations tested. Participants rated the most effective interventions less favorably.

That experiment predates current chatbots. It isn’t a verdict on every explanation; explanations can help in some conditions. But I take its finding as a reason to distinguish comfortable assistance from useful scrutiny.

My standard would be evidence suited to the decision: check the cited source, test the calculation, examine the assumption that could change the conclusion. The greater the consequence of an error, the stronger that check should be.

I don’t need a complete account of an AI’s internal workings to find its answer useful. I do need a reason to rely on it beyond how well it explains itself.
